title: Statement of Changes in Equity
description: Account for and present changes in contributed capital, retained earnings, accumulated OCI and other equity balances.
html:
Purpose of the statement of changes in equity

The statement of changes in equity explains how each major component of stockholders' equity changed during the reporting period.

At the CPA level, you should be able to connect transactions involving owners, net income, dividends, OCI and treasury stock to ending equity.

Main equity components can include

  • Common stock
  • Preferred stock
  • Additional paid-in capital
  • Retained earnings
  • Accumulated other comprehensive income or loss
  • Treasury stock

The basic retained earnings roll-forward

Beginning Retained Earnings + Net Income − Dividends ± Applicable Adjustments = Ending Retained Earnings

Beginning retained earnings: $300,000

Net income: $90,000

Dividends: $25,000

$300,000 + $90,000 − $25,000 = $365,000

CPA trap

Dividends reduce retained earnings, but they are not expenses and do not reduce net income.

Common stock and APIC

When shares are issued for cash, stockholders' equity generally increases.

A corporation issues 10,000 shares of $2 par common stock for $15 per share.

Cash received

10,000 × $15 = $150,000

Common stock

10,000 × $2 = $20,000

Additional paid-in capital

$150,000 − $20,000 = $130,000

Treasury stock

Treasury stock represents shares issued and later reacquired by the corporation.

Treasury stock is generally a contra-equity account and reduces total stockholders' equity.

A corporation repurchases 2,000 shares for $18 each.

2,000 × $18 = $36,000

Under the cost method, Treasury Stock is debited for $36,000.

CPA trap

Treasury stock is not an asset.

The corporation cannot create an asset simply by purchasing its own shares.

AOCI

Accumulated other comprehensive income captures the cumulative balance of OCI items that have not otherwise been reclassified or removed under the applicable guidance.

Beginning AOCI + Current-Period OCI ± Reclassification Adjustments = Ending AOCI

Owner transactions versus performance

The statement of changes in equity brings together both owner transactions and performance-related items.

Performance-related

Net income

Owner-related

Dividends

Treasury stock transactions

Full equity roll-forward example

Assume the following beginning balances:

Common Stock $100,000
APIC $250,000
Retained Earnings $400,000
AOCI $20,000
Treasury Stock ($50,000)

During the year:

  • Net income = $120,000
  • Dividends = $30,000
  • Current-period OCI gain = $15,000
  • New shares issued increase Common Stock by $10,000
  • The same issuance increases APIC by $60,000
  • Additional treasury stock is purchased for $25,000

Ending Common Stock

$100,000 + $10,000 = $110,000

Ending APIC

$250,000 + $60,000 = $310,000

Ending Retained Earnings

$400,000 + $120,000 − $30,000 = $490,000

Ending AOCI

$20,000 + $15,000 = $35,000

Ending Treasury Stock

($50,000) − $25,000 = ($75,000)

Ending Total Stockholders' Equity

$110,000 + $310,000 + $490,000 + $35,000 − $75,000 = $870,000

Relationship to the balance sheet

Ending balances from the statement of changes in equity flow into the equity section of the ending balance sheet.

This is another example of financial statement articulation.

What you should know after this lesson

  • Roll forward retained earnings.
  • Separate par value from APIC when shares are issued.
  • Understand treasury stock as contra-equity.
  • Understand how OCI affects AOCI.
  • Distinguish owner transactions from performance-related changes.
  • Connect ending equity balances to the balance sheet.

quiz.prompt: A corporation begins the year with $500,000 of retained earnings. During the year it reports $140,000 of net income and declares $45,000 of dividends. What is ending retained earnings?
quiz.explanation: Ending retained earnings equals beginning retained earnings plus net income minus dividends: $500,000 + $140,000 − $45,000 = $595,000.
